overview:
On 1 August 1929 a Prussian law redrew the map of the Rhenish-Westphalian industrial belt, and one of its clauses fused the neighbouring cities of Barmen and Elberfeld — long rivals strung along the same narrow valley of the river Wupper — with the towns of Cronenberg, Ronsdorf and Vohwinkel and pieces of seven other municipalities. The new municipality was at first called, awkwardly and without much affection, Barmen-Elberfeld; a decision in January 1930 replaced that hyphenated compromise with Wuppertal, "Wupper valley", a name that belonged to the geography rather than to either of the old rivals. The reform was not local sentiment but state policy. Prussia had amended its law in 1927 to permit boundary changes "for reasons of public welfare," and the Interior Ministry set planners to work on consolidating an industrial region whose municipal boundaries had been overtaken by its own sprawl. The legislation passed the Prussian parliament on 8 July 1929 over objections from the conservative DNVP and the DVP, was upheld by the state court weeks later, and reorganised three administrative districts at once, dissolving and creating whole counties in the process.

What was being merged mattered more than the merger's paperwork. The Wupper valley had been the first heavily industrialised region in Germany, a place of bleaching yards, ribbon and braid weaving, silk and later dyestuffs, chemicals and pharmaceuticals; Elberfeld had grown into the commercial and banking side of the pair while Barmen leaned toward manufacture. Its populations had multiplied in the early nineteenth century as workers streamed in, and the strains of that growth produced its own famous experiment in administration, the Elberfeld system of poor relief begun in 1853, in which volunteer visitors managed small caseloads of the poor — a model copied widely across Germany before mass urban poverty outgrew it. Barmen was the birthplace of Friedrich Engels in 1820, and the pious, hard-driving milieu of the valley's Protestant manufacturing families is part of what he was writing against.

By 1929 the valley also carried the object for which the city is still best known: the Schwebebahn, the suspended electric railway opened in 1901 and hung above the Wupper and its streets because the floor of the gorge had no room left for a conventional line. The merger gave that engineering oddity a single municipal owner, and gave a fragmented industrial corridor one budget, one administration and one name — four years before the Nazi seizure of power, and a decade and a half before Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed much of the built fabric the merger had just brought under one roof.
significance: The founding of Wuppertal is a small, legible instance of something that reshaped much of industrial Europe in the interwar decades: the recognition that the medieval and early-modern boundaries of towns no longer described where people actually lived and worked, and that the modern state could simply redraw them. The Prussian reform of 1929 was an exercise in rational spatial planning applied at scale, imposed from above against real local resistance, and the arguments it provoked — about lost autonomy, administrative economy and whether a merged city could acquire an identity — recur wherever governments have since amalgamated municipalities. That the resulting city took its name from a river rather than from either predecessor is a fair emblem of the whole transaction. And what was consolidated was itself historically weighty: the Wupper valley was Germany's earliest industrial district, an incubator of textile capitalism, of chemical and pharmaceutical industry, of an influential model of municipal welfare, and of the young Engels's disgust with all of it.
coverage: Written from the English and German Wikipedia accounts of the city and of the 1929 Prussian reorganisation law, plus reference-work summaries of Barmen, Elberfeld and the Elberfeld poor-relief system; the dataset itself holds no events for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped point. The administrative record of the merger is well documented in German municipal sources, but the texture of it is thin in what is readily available in English — how contested the merger was inside Barmen and Elberfeld, and the mechanics and margin of the 1930 decision on the name, are things I could not pin down here.
